title: SVM analysis links liquid ordering at interfaces to slower crystal growth
summary: A support-vector classifier of local atomic environments helped reveal how interface-induced ordering of liquid reduces atomic mobility and slows crystal growth in silicon and copper simulations. The learned structural quantity supported a growth model that predicted temperature-dependent rates beyond the fitted temperature range more effectively than the compared Wilson–Frenkel model. These are atomistic simulation and model-comparison results, with material/interface-specific limits rather than demonstrated industrial-process performance.
ai_technology: Support-vector machine encoding of local atomic environments

evidence.tested: SVM trained on 10,000 balanced atomic-environment examples; applied to 27.5 million held-out simulation data points. Crystal-growth models fitted at higher temperatures were compared against newly computed lower-temperature growth rates in silicon, with silicon/copper interface analyses.
evidence.unknown: Simulation results depend on the atomistic models and interfaces studied; general industrial applicability and independent experimental confirmation of the full learned mechanism were not established in this review.
evidence.ai_role: A trained SVM supplies a local structural softness coordinate that separates liquid/crystallizing environments and enables analysis of interface ordering, atom mobility and growth kinetics.
